notes.text: I create — I am about wholly to change the state not only of my people, but to bring a new face upon the world, which shall abide until a new heavens and earth appear, in which shall dwell nothing but righteousness. Not be remembered - That state of things shall be so glorious, that the former state of my people shall not be remembered.
You — The church, as well under the gospel, as under the law.

An infant — Those that were now children, shall die at a great age. But - Yet none of these things shall be of any advantage to wicked men, but if any of them shall live to be an hundred years old, yet they shall die accursed.
With them — Is blessed with them.

Before they call — God promised, chap. lviii, 9, to answer them, when they called: here he promises to answer the words, as soon as they should be formed in their hearts before they could get them out of their lips. While - Yea, while they were speaking.

The wolf, &c. — God here promises to take off the fierceness of the spirits of his peoples enemies, so that they shall live quietly and peaceably together. And dust - God promises a time of tranquility to his church under the metaphor of serpents eating the dust, their proper meat, Gen. iii, 14, instead of flying upon men: it signifies such a time, when wicked men shall no more eat up the people of God. God is served with the spirit, and not by ceremonies, ver. 1- 5. The wonderful birth and benefits of the gospel-church, ver. 6- 14. Severe judgments against the wicked, ver. 15-17. The Gentiles shall be an holy church, ver. 18-23. The eternal punishment of the wicked, ver. 24.

glossa.text: *For behold.* Out of angels, namely, and out of men, one Church; and they shall exult and rejoice, that I who created may exult and rejoice in them. *A rejoicing.* Of the whole earth, that she who of old was the joy of the Only-begotten may be, made new, a gladness to all nations. *A joy.* Which we can understand either after the resurrection, or after baptism in the first resurrection. This refers to the general resurrection in which all shall rise again in perfect age. And this is it: *There shall not be,* etc.

*A child of a hundred years,* etc. He, namely, who although he lived long, yet lived childishly, serving the vices: and Gregory expounds this thus. *A child of a hundred years. And a sinner of a hundred years.* The child's life is indeed drawn out long, that he may be corrected from childish deeds: but if he is not restrained from the perpetration of sin even by length of time, this very length of life, which he received through the mercy of God, grows for him unto a heap of malediction.
*Houses.* ((HIER.)) The virtues, for which they shall rest in the heavenly places, etc., *as far as* For many saints build houses, but do not dwell in them.
*For according to.* ((ID.)) As Christ etc., *as far as It is a tree of life to them that have laid hold on her,* namely on wisdom, which is Christ.

*The seed of the blessed.* The apostles, and other teachers in preaching, or in other works, as the Jews, because they shall receive an eternal reward, *for they shall come with joyfulness carrying their sheaves ((Psal. CXXV))*.

*Grandchildren.* Whom their sons have begotten in the faith, as Mark the disciple of Peter, and Luke the son of Paul.
*Before they call.* In trouble, in grief of mind, but in joy and gladness: whence, *For what is our joy or crown of glory, are not you ((II Thes. II))*? etc.

*The wolf.* The wolf is Saul, that is, the persecutor, of whom, *Benjamin a ravenous wolf ((Gen. XLIX))*. *The lamb.* Those, namely, who in white garments follow the lamb whithersoever he goes: of whom it is said to Peter, *Feed my lambs ((Joan. XXI))*. *And the lion and the ox shall eat.* A man, namely, eloquent and most powerful in the world, the eloquence of philosophy being despised, shall eat straw, that is, the usefulness and the surface of the history, with the oxen, that is, with the preachers of the Church. These things the lions eat until by many labours one comes to the depth of the mystery, as Augustine and Cyprian and the rest. *Neither shall they kill.* Their fierceness laid aside, either in the present or in the time to come, and this is it: *In all the mountain,* etc. This the Jews take carnally, saying that in the time of their own Christ there shall be for them so great peace and security that wolves and lambs, lions and oxen, serpents and men shall dwell together, and shall eat, nor shall they harm those who dwell in the temple and on the holy mountain. From which it is gathered that all the rest shall be killed. But that this is false is shown by these words: *Thus saith the Lord: Heaven is my seat, and the earth my footstool,* etc.; yet this too the Jews understand carnally.

notes.text: In that day — When this great work of the reduction of Israel, and conversion of the Gentiles is fulfilled.
God — My salvation hath not been brought to pass by man, but by the almighty power of God.

With joy — Your thirsty souls shall be filled with Divine graces and comforts, which you may draw from God, in the use of gospel-ordinances. God's armies, ver. 1-5. The destruction of Babylon by the Persians and Medes, their great distress, anguish, and utter desolation, ver. 6-22.

glossa.text: *I will give thanks to thee.* ((HIER.)) As, the Red Sea being passed, they said: Let us sing to the Lord, etc. So, the kingdom of the world being destroyed, the Church says: *I will give thanks to thee.*
*Out of the fountains of the Saviour.* ((ID.)) Whence: *Bless ye the Lord from the fountains of Israel,* etc., *as far as* that the prophecy may agree with the Gospel.

notes.text: That walketh disorderly — Particularly by not working. Not according to the tradition he received of us - The admonition we gave, both by word of mouth, and in our former epistle.
Neither let him eat — Do not maintain him in idleness.
Doing nothing, but being busybodies — To which idleness naturally disposes.
Work quietly — Letting the concerns of other people alone.

glossa.text: *We charge.* He begins concerning the curious and the idle, admonishing the good to correct them.

*You know how you ought to imitate us.* And since they do not these things, you ought to shun them. Or, they walk not according to the tradition. For you know how I bore myself, which you do not see in them; as if he should say: There is no need that I should expound to you that tradition, because you know it, namely that we were not restless, as those are who mind other men's business, wandering hither and thither.

*But that we ourselves.* It is to be noted that the Apostle taught not by words only, but exhorted also by deeds. For it belongs to a fit master to fulfil in works the things which he teaches in words.

*For if any man will not work.* Certain men say that the Apostle enjoined this concerning spiritual works; otherwise, if he said this of bodily work, in which either husbandmen or craftsmen labour, he would seem to hold an opinion against the Lord, who says in the Gospel: *Be not solicitous, what you shall eat* ((Matth. VI)), etc. But to no purpose do they strive to draw a mist over both themselves and others, so that they not only wish *velint* to do what charity profitably admonishes, but not even to understand it, since the Apostle in many other places of the epistles most plainly teaches what he here means. For he wills that the servants of God work bodily whereby they may live, that they be not compelled by want to beg for necessaries. Nor is this against that which was said before: *Be not solicitous what you shall eat,* etc. For this was not said to this end, that they should not procure as much as is enough for necessity, from whence they honourably could, but not in order that *sed non ut* they may look upon these things, nor do for the sake of these things whatever they are bidden to do by the proclamation of the Gospel.
*Curiously meddling.* The Lord's discipline abhors this deed, for their god is the belly, who with foul care provide necessaries for themselves.

*Faint not.* Because although they work, yet they may want some things. And therefore he admonishes, lest those who had wherewith to supply necessaries to the servants of God should on this occasion grow slothful. For he does not come under reproof who is kindly in bestowing, but he who, when he could bear labour, wishes to lead his life in idleness.

notes.text: Goodly stones — Such as no engines now in use could have brought, or even set upon each other. Some of them (as an eye witness who lately measured them writes) were forty - five cubits long, five high, and six broad; yet brought thither from another country. And gifts - Which persons delivered from imminent dangers had, in accomplishment of their vows, hung on the walls and pillars. The marble of the temple was so white, that it appeared like a mountain of snow at a distance. And the gilding of many parts made it, especially when the sun shone, a most splendid and beautiful spectacle. Matt. xxiv, 1; Mark xiii, 1.
I am the Christ; and the time is near — When I will deliver you from all your enemies. They are the words of the seducers.
Commotions — Intestine broils; civil wars.
Fearful sights and signs from heaven — Of which Josephus gives a circumstantial account.
Mark xiii, 9.
It shall turn to you for a testimony — Of your having delivered your own souls, and of their being without excuse.
Matt. x, 21.
Matt. xxiv, 13; Mark xiii, 13.
Not a hair of your head — A proverbial expression, shall perish - Without the special providence of God. And then, not before the time, nor without a full reward.

In your patience possess ye your souls — Be calm and serene, masters of yourselves, and superior to all irrational and disquieting passions. By keeping the government of your spirits, you will both avoid much misery, and guard the better against all dangers.

glossa.text: *And some.* After the widow's offering, in which the Church of the Gentiles is signified, the destruction of the temple is subjoined, so that, with the veil of the concealing letter, the hidden sacraments of the Church may begin to be disclosed. For God took care to overthrow the city and the temple and all figurative things, lest anyone after the coming of Christ should run back to them.

*They asked him.* Because to those praising the buildings of the temple he had foretold that all was to be destroyed, the disciples (as Mark says), Peter, James, and John and Andrew, ask apart the time and the signs of the foretold destruction.

*For many.* When the destruction of Jerusalem was at hand, there were many leaders who said that they were Christs and that the time of liberty was drawing near. In the times of the apostles also many heresiarchs came forth, who among their other falsehoods preached that the day of the Lord was at hand, whom the Apostle also refuted.

*Wars and seditions.* These abounded in Judaea from the passion of the Lord; and lest the apostles, terrified by them, should forsake Jerusalem and Judaea, they are warned *that the end is not immediately,* but after the forty-second year.

*Then he said.* Of these, some are from heaven, some from the earth, some from the elements, some from men. Mystically. Kingdom against kingdom, and the pestilence of those whose speech creeps like a canker, and the famine of hearing the word of God, the shaking of the earth, the separation from the true faith, ought to be understood of heretics, who, fighting against one another, make the victory of the Church. *And great signs.* These also are found fulfilled at that time in Josephus, who relates that a star like a sword hung over Jerusalem for a year, and that chariots and armed horsemen fought in the air for forty days, and that a heifer brought forth a lamb among the hands of those sacrificing.

*And it shall happen,* etc. Of those who either persecute, or are not changed by their living. For the death of the just is to the good a help, to the wicked a testimony of damnation, so that the perverse may perish without excuse from that whence the elect take an example that they may live.

*By parents,* etc. It is a greater torment when a man suffers from those upon whom he counted, because along with the loss of the body the evils of lost charity torment him. And because the things foretold of the affliction of death are hard, a consolation concerning the joy of the resurrection is subjoined.

*And a hair.* As if he said: Why do you fear that that should perish which hurts when cut, seeing that not even there can that perish in you which does not hurt when cut? For the flesh when cut hurts, the hair does not hurt.

*In your patience.* Patience is the root and the guardian of all the virtues. In it therefore we possess our souls, which possess the body, when we govern those souls by reason unto suffering. But true patience is to endure with equanimity the evils of another, and to be moved by no grief against him who inflicts the evils.

echoes.text: By the sweat of your face will you eat bread until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken. For you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”
echoes.note: 'If anyone will not work, neither let him eat' rests on the primeval verdict that by the sweat of your face you shall eat bread. The post-Eden link between toil and bread is the theological ground of Paul's labor rule, including his own working night and day for his bread.

echoes.text: He becomes poor who works with a lazy hand, but the hand of the diligent brings wealth.
echoes.note: The wisdom contrast between the slack/idle hand bringing poverty and the diligent hand bringing wealth underlies Paul's rebuke of those who refuse to work. Proverbs' sustained ethic of diligence vs. sloth shapes his command.

echoes.text: Go to the ant, you sluggard. Consider her ways, and be wise; which having no chief, overseer, or ruler, provides her bread in the summer, and gathers her food in the harvest. How long will you sleep, sluggard? When will you arise out of your sleep? A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep: so your poverty will come as a robber, and your scarcity as an armed man.
echoes.note: The sluggard sent to the ant, who provides her food by labor, and the warning that poverty comes on the lazy, parallels Paul's portrait of the idle who refuse to work. A central sloth-condemning passage in the wisdom tradition.

echoes.text: Send him to labor, that he be not idle; For idleness teaches much mischief. Set him to work, as is fit for him; And if he obey not, make his fetters heavy.
echoes.note: Ben Sira urges putting an idle servant to work lest idleness teach mischief, since idleness breeds trouble. This deuterocanonical labor wisdom is close in spirit to Paul's treatment of the idle who become busybodies.

echoes.text: Slothfulness casts into a deep sleep. The idle soul shall suffer hunger.
echoes.note: 'Idleness casts into a deep sleep, and the slack person will go hungry' closely mirrors Paul's pairing of idleness with not eating. A pointed wisdom maxim on the cost of laziness.

echoes.text: One who works his land will have an abundance of food; but one who chases fantasies will have his fill of poverty.
echoes.note: 'Whoever works his land will have plenty of bread, but he who follows worthless pursuits will have plenty of poverty' echoes Paul's bread-and-work logic and his complaint about busybodies pursuing nothing useful.

echoes.text: But those who wait for Yahweh will renew their strength. They will mount up with wings like eagles. They will run, and not be weary. They will walk, and not faint.
echoes.note: 'Don't be weary in doing well' may echo Isaiah's promise that those who wait on the Lord will renew strength, run and not be weary, walk and not faint. The shared vocabulary of not growing weary is suggestive but the Isaian context is endurance, not active well-doing.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Therefore Zion for your sake will be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem will become heaps of rubble, and the mountain of the temple like the high places of a forest.
echoes.note: Micah prophesies that Zion will be plowed as a field and Jerusalem become heaps, the temple mount a wooded height, the classic oracle of the temple's destruction quoted at Jeremiah 26:18. Jesus' prediction that not one stone will be left on another draws directly on this prophetic tradition of the sanctuary leveled for the people's injustice. High coherence with Luke's broader judgment-on-Jerusalem theme.

echoes.text: then I will make this house like Shiloh, and will make this city a curse to all the nations of the earth.
echoes.note: Jeremiah threatens to make the temple like Shiloh and the city a curse, citing Micah's Zion-plowed oracle in a temple sermon that nearly costs him his life. Luke frames Jesus' temple-destruction saying in the same setting (teaching in the temple, opposed by leaders), echoing the prophet who foretold the first temple's fall. Strong recurrence of the temple-doom motif.

echoes.text: Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes? Behold, I, even I, have seen it,” says Yahweh. “But go now to my place which was in Shiloh, where I caused my name to dwell at the first, and see what I did to it for the wickedness of my people Israel. Now, because you have done all these works,” says Yahweh, “and I spoke to you, rising up early and speaking, but you didn’t hear; and I called you, but you didn’t answer: […]
echoes.note: Jeremiah's temple sermon warns that God will do to this house, called by his name, as he did to Shiloh, because the people made it a den of robbers. Luke has just narrated Jesus quoting Jer 7:11 in the temple cleansing (19:46), so the threatened destruction of the desecrated house carries forward here. Coherence and recurrence within Luke's temple sequence.

echoes.text: then I will cut off Israel out of the land which I have given them; and this house, which I have made holy for my name, will I cast out of my sight; and Israel shall be a proverb and a byword among all peoples. Though this house is so high, yet shall everyone who passes by it be astonished, and shall hiss; and they shall say, ‘Why has Yahweh done thus to this land, and to this house?’
echoes.note: The Lord warns Solomon that if Israel turns away he will cast off the house he has hallowed and it will become a heap of ruins, an astonishment, with passersby hissing. The admiration of the temple's beautiful stones immediately before the announcement of its fall mirrors this conditional doom on the very house just dedicated. Thematic coherence with the temple-destruction prophecies.

echoes.text: ‘The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former,’ says Yahweh of Armies; ‘and in this place will I give peace,’ says Yahweh of Armies.”
echoes.note: Haggai promises the latter glory of this house, adorned with the wealth of nations, will exceed the former. The disciples' marveling at the temple's beautiful stones and votive gifts evokes that anticipated splendor, which Jesus then declares doomed. Faint ironic counterpoint rather than citation.

echoes.text: They were broken in pieces, nation against nation, and city against city; for God troubled them with all adversity.
echoes.note: Azariah's oracle: 'nation was crushed by nation and city by city, for God troubled them with every distress.' Jesus' 'nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom' is the closest verbal parallel in the OT, framing political chaos as divine eschatological distress. High volume and coherence.

echoes.text: I will stir up the Egyptians against the Egyptians, and they will fight everyone against his brother, and everyone against his neighbor; city against city, and kingdom against kingdom.
echoes.note: Isaiah's oracle against Egypt: 'I will stir up Egyptians against Egyptians, and they will fight, everyone against his brother and against his neighbor, city against city, kingdom against kingdom.' The kingdom-against-kingdom formula and the picture of internecine collapse map directly onto Jesus' words. Strong verbal recurrence.

echoes.text: but there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets, and he has made known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Your dream, and the visions of your head on your bed, are these: as for you, O king, your thoughts came on your bed, what should happen hereafter; and he who reveals secrets has made known to you what shall happen.
echoes.note: Daniel speaks of what 'must happen' (dei genesthai) in the latter days, language Jesus reuses verbatim in 'these things must happen first.' Daniel's apocalyptic framework of divinely-decreed end-time events shapes the whole discourse's logic of necessity. Strong verbal coherence with Danielic apocalyptic.

echoes.text: Therefore I will make the heavens tremble, and the earth will be shaken out of its place in the wrath of Yahweh of Armies, and in the day of his fierce anger.
echoes.note: In the Day-of-the-Lord oracle against Babylon, the heavens tremble and the earth is shaken out of its place in God's wrath. Jesus' great earthquakes and 'terrors and great signs from heaven' draw on this Day-of-the-Lord seismic and celestial imagery. Coherence with the prophetic eschatological catalog.

echoes.text: For in my jealousy and in the fire of my wrath have I spoken, Surely in that day there shall be a great shaking in the land of Israel; so that the fish of the sea, and the birds of the sky, and the animals of the field, and all creeping things who creep on the earth, and all the men who are on the surface of the earth, shall shake at my presence, and the mountains shall be thrown down, and the steep places shall fall, and every wall shall fall to the […]
echoes.note: In the Gog oracle a great earthquake shakes the land, with pestilence, bloodshed, famine, and signs of God's judgment. The clustering of earthquake, plague, and famine as eschatological signs parallels Jesus' list closely. Recurrence of the standard Day-of-the-Lord disaster catalog.

echoes.text: When they fast, I will not hear their cry; and when they offer burnt offering and meal offering, I will not accept them; but I will consume them by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence.
echoes.note: Jeremiah names sword, famine, and pestilence (plague) as the triad by which God consumes the people, a formula repeated dozens of times in the prophet. Jesus' famines and plagues echo this fixed prophetic triad of covenant curse. Strong recurrence across Jeremiah and Ezekiel.

echoes.text: I will show wonders in the heavens and in the earth: blood, fire, and pillars of smoke. The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: Joel promises wonders in heaven and on earth as portents of the Day of the Lord. Jesus' 'great signs from heaven' belongs to this Joel tradition of celestial portents, developed more fully later in the discourse. Coherence with Joel's sign vocabulary.

echoes.text: But news out of the east and out of the north shall trouble him; and he shall go out with great fury to destroy and utterly to sweep away many.
echoes.note: Rumors and reports of war from east and north alarm the eschatological king and provoke great fury. Jesus' 'when you hear of wars and disturbances, don't be terrified' echoes the apocalyptic motif of unsettling war-reports that must not panic the faithful. Faint Danielic coloring.

echoes.text: They will fight against you; but they will not prevail against you; for I am with you”, says Yahweh, “to deliver you.”
echoes.note: God assures the prophet that kings and officials will fight against him but 'shall not prevail against you, for I am with you to deliver you.' Jesus' promise that adversaries 'will not be able to withstand or to contradict' the wisdom he gives mirrors this prophetic commissioning against hostile authorities. High coherence with the persecuted-prophet pattern.

echoes.text: Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth, and teach you what you shall speak.”
echoes.note: God tells Moses, 'I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak.' Jesus' 'I will give you a mouth and wisdom' directly evokes this divine endowment of speech to a reluctant spokesman before a hostile king. Strong verbal and situational coherence.

echoes.text: For the son dishonors the father, the daughter rises up against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man’s enemies are the men of his own house.
echoes.note: Micah laments that son dishonors father, daughter rises against mother, and a man's enemies are those of his own household. Jesus' 'you will be handed over even by parents, brothers, relatives, and friends' draws on this prophetic image of eschatological family betrayal. Strong coherence and recurrence in Synoptic tradition.

echoes.text: The people said to Saul, “Shall Jonathan die, who has worked this great salvation in Israel? Far from it! As Yahweh lives, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground; for he has worked with God this day!” So the people rescued Jonathan, that he didn’t die.
echoes.note: The people swear that not one hair of Jonathan's head shall fall to the ground, for he has worked with God this day, sparing his life. Jesus' 'not a hair of your head will perish' is a near-verbatim proverbial assurance of divine preservation. High volume on the distinctive idiom.

echoes.text: You shall speak to him, and put the words in his mouth. I will be with your mouth, and with his mouth, and will teach you what you shall do. He will be your spokesman to the people; and it will happen, that he will be to you a mouth, and you will be to him as God.
echoes.note: The Lord promises to be with the mouth of both Moses and Aaron and to teach them what to do, the divine-rhetoric motif extended. The doubling of mouth-and-teaching reinforces the Exodus background of God supplying words to those summoned before rulers. Recurrence strengthens the Mosaic echo.

echoes.text: Then answered they and said before the king, That Daniel, who is of the children of the captivity of Judah, doesn’t respect you, O king, nor the decree that you have signed, but makes his petition three times a day. Then the king, when he heard these words, was very displeased, and set his heart on Daniel to deliver him; and he labored until the going down of the sun to rescue him. Then these men assembled together to the king, and said to the king, Know, […]
echoes.note: Daniel is brought before the king and delivered up on account of his fidelity, a model of the faithful Jew arraigned before pagan authority who is nonetheless preserved. Jesus' 'bringing you before kings and governors for my name's sake' as occasion for testimony evokes the Danielic court-confessor tradition. Coherence with Daniel's witness motif.

echoes.text: He shall speak words against the Most High, and shall wear out the saints of the Most High; and he shall think to change the times and the law; and they shall be given into his hand until a time and times and half a time.
echoes.note: The little horn wears out the saints of the Most High, who are given into his hand for a time. Jesus' forecast of persecution, betrayal, and death of his followers fits the Danielic pattern of the saints handed over before final vindication. Recurrence within the apocalyptic source of the discourse.

echoes.text: Then she said, “Please let the king remember Yahweh your God, that the avenger of blood destroy not any more, lest they destroy my son.” He said, “As Yahweh lives, not one hair of your son shall fall to the earth.”
echoes.note: The wise woman of Tekoa secures David's oath that 'not one hair of your son shall fall to the ground,' the same idiom of total protection. The recurrence of the hair-of-the-head formula across Samuel reinforces its proverbial status behind Jesus' saying. Coherence with the OT preservation idiom.

echoes.text: Solomon said, “If he shows himself a worthy man, not a hair of him shall fall to the earth; but if wickedness be found in him, he shall die.”
echoes.note: Solomon declares that if Adonijah proves worthy, 'not one of his hairs shall fall to the earth.' A third occurrence of the hair-preservation formula, confirming it as a fixed Hebrew idiom Jesus deploys. Faint but corroborating recurrence.

echoes.text: Blessed is he who waits, and comes to the one thousand three hundred thirty-five days. But go you your way until the end; for you shall rest, and shall stand in your lot, at the end of the days.
echoes.note: Daniel is told, 'blessed is he who waits' and to stand in his lot at the end of days, framing endurance as the path to eschatological reward. Jesus' 'by your endurance you will win your lives' resonates with this Danielic call to persevere to the resurrection-end. Thematic coherence with apocalyptic endurance.

notes.text: Cometh — Tho' it be at a distance from you, yet it is coming and will overtake you and overwhelm you too. As an oven - The refiner's fire, chap. iii, 2, is now represented as a fire, burning more dreadfully, as it did indeed when Jerusalem and the temple were on fire, when the fire raged everywhere, but most fiercely where the arched roofs made it double itself, and infold flames with flames. And this may well be an emblem of the day of judgment.

The sun of righteousness — Christ, who is fitly compared to the sun, being the fountain of light, and vital heat to his church. And of mercy and benignity; for the Hebrew word imports both. With healing - His beams shall bring health and strength, with delight and joy, safety and security. Go forth - Go out of Jerusalem, before the fatal siege. Grow up - In strength, vigour and spiritual stature. Of the stall - Where they are safe guarded and well ordered.

Salvation — The redemption of the world by the Messiah: which was hitherto reserved was a secret among the Jews, yea was not throughly known by the most of the Jews themselves. Righteousness - His faithfulness in accomplishing this great promise. Israel is required to praise God, for their hasty constitution both in church and state, ver. 1-5. Some instances of the happy administration of it, ver. 6-9.

glossa.text:
*Sing ye to the Lord.* ((CASS.)) First he speaks of the showing forth of the saving right hand.

*He hath saved.* ((AUG.)) It is a greater thing that he raised up the whole world from eternal death, than that he raised the dead. *To himself.* Many are saved bodily, but to themselves, not to him: they who, having received bodily health, grow wanton, but they who by faith are healed within, are healed to him, or save themselves.

*Salvation . . . justice.* ((AUG.)) He who saves and justifies. *He hath revealed.* Things to come were foretold under a veil by the prophets: but the veil has been taken away, since *truth is sprung out of the earth.*

*Of mercy and of truth.* ((AUG.)) *Mercy* is that whereby he promised, *truth* follows upon this, because he rendered it. But to whom? *To Israel,* that is, to him who now by faith sees the truth, afterwards by sight.
*All.* ((ID.)) Because Christ was not given to certain men only.
*Rejoice ye.* ((CASS.)) Secondly he says that in all ways he is to be praised and declared, because the judge is come.

*With ductile trumpets and with the voice of a trumpet of horn.* ((AUG.)) Of brass, which are drawn out by beating, etc., *as far as* as the horn cleaves to the flesh, and surpasses it. ((HIERON.)) With ductile trumpets, of silver, after the manner of the Jews. Mystically, drawn out under the hammer of the whole earth, that is, the devil. ((AUG.)) Tribulation is the beating; advancement, the drawing out: such a trumpet was Job, whence he sounded as a trumpet, saying: *The Lord gave, the Lord hath taken away.*

*Let it be moved.* ((ID.)) That is, let the sea of the law be made sweet, the wood of the cross being set therein. *And the fulness thereof.* All the sacraments of the law, etc., *as far as* but *the rivers,* etc. *The earth.* ((CASS.)) That is, every sinner.

*The world of the earth.* All earthly men. *In justice.* ((AUG.)) Because they did not merit mercy. *The peoples.* ((CASS.)) The faithful out of the Jews and the Gentiles, who shall receive things equal to their merits.

notes.text: That walketh disorderly — Particularly by not working. Not according to the tradition he received of us - The admonition we gave, both by word of mouth, and in our former epistle.
Neither let him eat — Do not maintain him in idleness.
Doing nothing, but being busybodies — To which idleness naturally disposes.
Work quietly — Letting the concerns of other people alone.

glossa.text: *We charge.* He begins concerning the curious and the idle, admonishing the good to correct them.

*You know how you ought to imitate us.* And since they do not these things, you ought to shun them. Or, they walk not according to the tradition. For you know how I bore myself, which you do not see in them; as if he should say: There is no need that I should expound to you that tradition, because you know it, namely that we were not restless, as those are who mind other men's business, wandering hither and thither.

*But that we ourselves.* It is to be noted that the Apostle taught not by words only, but exhorted also by deeds. For it belongs to a fit master to fulfil in works the things which he teaches in words.

*For if any man will not work.* Certain men say that the Apostle enjoined this concerning spiritual works; otherwise, if he said this of bodily work, in which either husbandmen or craftsmen labour, he would seem to hold an opinion against the Lord, who says in the Gospel: *Be not solicitous, what you shall eat* ((Matth. VI)), etc. But to no purpose do they strive to draw a mist over both themselves and others, so that they not only wish *velint* to do what charity profitably admonishes, but not even to understand it, since the Apostle in many other places of the epistles most plainly teaches what he here means. For he wills that the servants of God work bodily whereby they may live, that they be not compelled by want to beg for necessaries. Nor is this against that which was said before: *Be not solicitous what you shall eat,* etc. For this was not said to this end, that they should not procure as much as is enough for necessity, from whence they honourably could, but not in order that *sed non ut* they may look upon these things, nor do for the sake of these things whatever they are bidden to do by the proclamation of the Gospel.
*Curiously meddling.* The Lord's discipline abhors this deed, for their god is the belly, who with foul care provide necessaries for themselves.

*Faint not.* Because although they work, yet they may want some things. And therefore he admonishes, lest those who had wherewith to supply necessaries to the servants of God should on this occasion grow slothful. For he does not come under reproof who is kindly in bestowing, but he who, when he could bear labour, wishes to lead his life in idleness.

notes.text: Goodly stones — Such as no engines now in use could have brought, or even set upon each other. Some of them (as an eye witness who lately measured them writes) were forty - five cubits long, five high, and six broad; yet brought thither from another country. And gifts - Which persons delivered from imminent dangers had, in accomplishment of their vows, hung on the walls and pillars. The marble of the temple was so white, that it appeared like a mountain of snow at a distance. And the gilding of many parts made it, especially when the sun shone, a most splendid and beautiful spectacle. Matt. xxiv, 1; Mark xiii, 1.
I am the Christ; and the time is near — When I will deliver you from all your enemies. They are the words of the seducers.
Commotions — Intestine broils; civil wars.
Fearful sights and signs from heaven — Of which Josephus gives a circumstantial account.
Mark xiii, 9.
It shall turn to you for a testimony — Of your having delivered your own souls, and of their being without excuse.
Matt. x, 21.
Matt. xxiv, 13; Mark xiii, 13.
Not a hair of your head — A proverbial expression, shall perish - Without the special providence of God. And then, not before the time, nor without a full reward.

In your patience possess ye your souls — Be calm and serene, masters of yourselves, and superior to all irrational and disquieting passions. By keeping the government of your spirits, you will both avoid much misery, and guard the better against all dangers.

glossa.text: *And some.* After the widow's offering, in which the Church of the Gentiles is signified, the destruction of the temple is subjoined, so that, with the veil of the concealing letter, the hidden sacraments of the Church may begin to be disclosed. For God took care to overthrow the city and the temple and all figurative things, lest anyone after the coming of Christ should run back to them.

*They asked him.* Because to those praising the buildings of the temple he had foretold that all was to be destroyed, the disciples (as Mark says), Peter, James, and John and Andrew, ask apart the time and the signs of the foretold destruction.

*For many.* When the destruction of Jerusalem was at hand, there were many leaders who said that they were Christs and that the time of liberty was drawing near. In the times of the apostles also many heresiarchs came forth, who among their other falsehoods preached that the day of the Lord was at hand, whom the Apostle also refuted.

*Wars and seditions.* These abounded in Judaea from the passion of the Lord; and lest the apostles, terrified by them, should forsake Jerusalem and Judaea, they are warned *that the end is not immediately,* but after the forty-second year.

*Then he said.* Of these, some are from heaven, some from the earth, some from the elements, some from men. Mystically. Kingdom against kingdom, and the pestilence of those whose speech creeps like a canker, and the famine of hearing the word of God, the shaking of the earth, the separation from the true faith, ought to be understood of heretics, who, fighting against one another, make the victory of the Church. *And great signs.* These also are found fulfilled at that time in Josephus, who relates that a star like a sword hung over Jerusalem for a year, and that chariots and armed horsemen fought in the air for forty days, and that a heifer brought forth a lamb among the hands of those sacrificing.

*And it shall happen,* etc. Of those who either persecute, or are not changed by their living. For the death of the just is to the good a help, to the wicked a testimony of damnation, so that the perverse may perish without excuse from that whence the elect take an example that they may live.

*By parents,* etc. It is a greater torment when a man suffers from those upon whom he counted, because along with the loss of the body the evils of lost charity torment him. And because the things foretold of the affliction of death are hard, a consolation concerning the joy of the resurrection is subjoined.

*And a hair.* As if he said: Why do you fear that that should perish which hurts when cut, seeing that not even there can that perish in you which does not hurt when cut? For the flesh when cut hurts, the hair does not hurt.

*In your patience.* Patience is the root and the guardian of all the virtues. In it therefore we possess our souls, which possess the body, when we govern those souls by reason unto suffering. But true patience is to endure with equanimity the evils of another, and to be moved by no grief against him who inflicts the evils.

echoes.text: By the sweat of your face will you eat bread until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken. For you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”
echoes.note: 'If anyone will not work, neither let him eat' rests on the primeval verdict that by the sweat of your face you shall eat bread. The post-Eden link between toil and bread is the theological ground of Paul's labor rule, including his own working night and day for his bread.

echoes.text: He becomes poor who works with a lazy hand, but the hand of the diligent brings wealth.
echoes.note: The wisdom contrast between the slack/idle hand bringing poverty and the diligent hand bringing wealth underlies Paul's rebuke of those who refuse to work. Proverbs' sustained ethic of diligence vs. sloth shapes his command.

echoes.text: Go to the ant, you sluggard. Consider her ways, and be wise; which having no chief, overseer, or ruler, provides her bread in the summer, and gathers her food in the harvest. How long will you sleep, sluggard? When will you arise out of your sleep? A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep: so your poverty will come as a robber, and your scarcity as an armed man.
echoes.note: The sluggard sent to the ant, who provides her food by labor, and the warning that poverty comes on the lazy, parallels Paul's portrait of the idle who refuse to work. A central sloth-condemning passage in the wisdom tradition.

echoes.text: Send him to labor, that he be not idle; For idleness teaches much mischief. Set him to work, as is fit for him; And if he obey not, make his fetters heavy.
echoes.note: Ben Sira urges putting an idle servant to work lest idleness teach mischief, since idleness breeds trouble. This deuterocanonical labor wisdom is close in spirit to Paul's treatment of the idle who become busybodies.

echoes.text: Slothfulness casts into a deep sleep. The idle soul shall suffer hunger.
echoes.note: 'Idleness casts into a deep sleep, and the slack person will go hungry' closely mirrors Paul's pairing of idleness with not eating. A pointed wisdom maxim on the cost of laziness.

echoes.text: One who works his land will have an abundance of food; but one who chases fantasies will have his fill of poverty.
echoes.note: 'Whoever works his land will have plenty of bread, but he who follows worthless pursuits will have plenty of poverty' echoes Paul's bread-and-work logic and his complaint about busybodies pursuing nothing useful.

echoes.text: But those who wait for Yahweh will renew their strength. They will mount up with wings like eagles. They will run, and not be weary. They will walk, and not faint.
echoes.note: 'Don't be weary in doing well' may echo Isaiah's promise that those who wait on the Lord will renew strength, run and not be weary, walk and not faint. The shared vocabulary of not growing weary is suggestive but the Isaian context is endurance, not active well-doing.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Therefore Zion for your sake will be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem will become heaps of rubble, and the mountain of the temple like the high places of a forest.
echoes.note: Micah prophesies that Zion will be plowed as a field and Jerusalem become heaps, the temple mount a wooded height, the classic oracle of the temple's destruction quoted at Jeremiah 26:18. Jesus' prediction that not one stone will be left on another draws directly on this prophetic tradition of the sanctuary leveled for the people's injustice. High coherence with Luke's broader judgment-on-Jerusalem theme.

echoes.text: then I will make this house like Shiloh, and will make this city a curse to all the nations of the earth.
echoes.note: Jeremiah threatens to make the temple like Shiloh and the city a curse, citing Micah's Zion-plowed oracle in a temple sermon that nearly costs him his life. Luke frames Jesus' temple-destruction saying in the same setting (teaching in the temple, opposed by leaders), echoing the prophet who foretold the first temple's fall. Strong recurrence of the temple-doom motif.

echoes.text: Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes? Behold, I, even I, have seen it,” says Yahweh. “But go now to my place which was in Shiloh, where I caused my name to dwell at the first, and see what I did to it for the wickedness of my people Israel. Now, because you have done all these works,” says Yahweh, “and I spoke to you, rising up early and speaking, but you didn’t hear; and I called you, but you didn’t answer: […]
echoes.note: Jeremiah's temple sermon warns that God will do to this house, called by his name, as he did to Shiloh, because the people made it a den of robbers. Luke has just narrated Jesus quoting Jer 7:11 in the temple cleansing (19:46), so the threatened destruction of the desecrated house carries forward here. Coherence and recurrence within Luke's temple sequence.

echoes.text: then I will cut off Israel out of the land which I have given them; and this house, which I have made holy for my name, will I cast out of my sight; and Israel shall be a proverb and a byword among all peoples. Though this house is so high, yet shall everyone who passes by it be astonished, and shall hiss; and they shall say, ‘Why has Yahweh done thus to this land, and to this house?’
echoes.note: The Lord warns Solomon that if Israel turns away he will cast off the house he has hallowed and it will become a heap of ruins, an astonishment, with passersby hissing. The admiration of the temple's beautiful stones immediately before the announcement of its fall mirrors this conditional doom on the very house just dedicated. Thematic coherence with the temple-destruction prophecies.

echoes.text: ‘The latter glory of this house will be greater than the former,’ says Yahweh of Armies; ‘and in this place will I give peace,’ says Yahweh of Armies.”
echoes.note: Haggai promises the latter glory of this house, adorned with the wealth of nations, will exceed the former. The disciples' marveling at the temple's beautiful stones and votive gifts evokes that anticipated splendor, which Jesus then declares doomed. Faint ironic counterpoint rather than citation.

echoes.text: They were broken in pieces, nation against nation, and city against city; for God troubled them with all adversity.
echoes.note: Azariah's oracle: 'nation was crushed by nation and city by city, for God troubled them with every distress.' Jesus' 'nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom' is the closest verbal parallel in the OT, framing political chaos as divine eschatological distress. High volume and coherence.

echoes.text: I will stir up the Egyptians against the Egyptians, and they will fight everyone against his brother, and everyone against his neighbor; city against city, and kingdom against kingdom.
echoes.note: Isaiah's oracle against Egypt: 'I will stir up Egyptians against Egyptians, and they will fight, everyone against his brother and against his neighbor, city against city, kingdom against kingdom.' The kingdom-against-kingdom formula and the picture of internecine collapse map directly onto Jesus' words. Strong verbal recurrence.

echoes.text: but there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets, and he has made known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Your dream, and the visions of your head on your bed, are these: as for you, O king, your thoughts came on your bed, what should happen hereafter; and he who reveals secrets has made known to you what shall happen.
echoes.note: Daniel speaks of what 'must happen' (dei genesthai) in the latter days, language Jesus reuses verbatim in 'these things must happen first.' Daniel's apocalyptic framework of divinely-decreed end-time events shapes the whole discourse's logic of necessity. Strong verbal coherence with Danielic apocalyptic.

echoes.text: Therefore I will make the heavens tremble, and the earth will be shaken out of its place in the wrath of Yahweh of Armies, and in the day of his fierce anger.
echoes.note: In the Day-of-the-Lord oracle against Babylon, the heavens tremble and the earth is shaken out of its place in God's wrath. Jesus' great earthquakes and 'terrors and great signs from heaven' draw on this Day-of-the-Lord seismic and celestial imagery. Coherence with the prophetic eschatological catalog.

echoes.text: For in my jealousy and in the fire of my wrath have I spoken, Surely in that day there shall be a great shaking in the land of Israel; so that the fish of the sea, and the birds of the sky, and the animals of the field, and all creeping things who creep on the earth, and all the men who are on the surface of the earth, shall shake at my presence, and the mountains shall be thrown down, and the steep places shall fall, and every wall shall fall to the […]
echoes.note: In the Gog oracle a great earthquake shakes the land, with pestilence, bloodshed, famine, and signs of God's judgment. The clustering of earthquake, plague, and famine as eschatological signs parallels Jesus' list closely. Recurrence of the standard Day-of-the-Lord disaster catalog.

echoes.text: When they fast, I will not hear their cry; and when they offer burnt offering and meal offering, I will not accept them; but I will consume them by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence.
echoes.note: Jeremiah names sword, famine, and pestilence (plague) as the triad by which God consumes the people, a formula repeated dozens of times in the prophet. Jesus' famines and plagues echo this fixed prophetic triad of covenant curse. Strong recurrence across Jeremiah and Ezekiel.

echoes.text: I will show wonders in the heavens and in the earth: blood, fire, and pillars of smoke. The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: Joel promises wonders in heaven and on earth as portents of the Day of the Lord. Jesus' 'great signs from heaven' belongs to this Joel tradition of celestial portents, developed more fully later in the discourse. Coherence with Joel's sign vocabulary.

echoes.text: But news out of the east and out of the north shall trouble him; and he shall go out with great fury to destroy and utterly to sweep away many.
echoes.note: Rumors and reports of war from east and north alarm the eschatological king and provoke great fury. Jesus' 'when you hear of wars and disturbances, don't be terrified' echoes the apocalyptic motif of unsettling war-reports that must not panic the faithful. Faint Danielic coloring.

echoes.text: They will fight against you; but they will not prevail against you; for I am with you”, says Yahweh, “to deliver you.”
echoes.note: God assures the prophet that kings and officials will fight against him but 'shall not prevail against you, for I am with you to deliver you.' Jesus' promise that adversaries 'will not be able to withstand or to contradict' the wisdom he gives mirrors this prophetic commissioning against hostile authorities. High coherence with the persecuted-prophet pattern.

echoes.text: Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth, and teach you what you shall speak.”
echoes.note: God tells Moses, 'I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak.' Jesus' 'I will give you a mouth and wisdom' directly evokes this divine endowment of speech to a reluctant spokesman before a hostile king. Strong verbal and situational coherence.

echoes.text: For the son dishonors the father, the daughter rises up against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man’s enemies are the men of his own house.
echoes.note: Micah laments that son dishonors father, daughter rises against mother, and a man's enemies are those of his own household. Jesus' 'you will be handed over even by parents, brothers, relatives, and friends' draws on this prophetic image of eschatological family betrayal. Strong coherence and recurrence in Synoptic tradition.

echoes.text: The people said to Saul, “Shall Jonathan die, who has worked this great salvation in Israel? Far from it! As Yahweh lives, there shall not one hair of his head fall to the ground; for he has worked with God this day!” So the people rescued Jonathan, that he didn’t die.
echoes.note: The people swear that not one hair of Jonathan's head shall fall to the ground, for he has worked with God this day, sparing his life. Jesus' 'not a hair of your head will perish' is a near-verbatim proverbial assurance of divine preservation. High volume on the distinctive idiom.

echoes.text: You shall speak to him, and put the words in his mouth. I will be with your mouth, and with his mouth, and will teach you what you shall do. He will be your spokesman to the people; and it will happen, that he will be to you a mouth, and you will be to him as God.
echoes.note: The Lord promises to be with the mouth of both Moses and Aaron and to teach them what to do, the divine-rhetoric motif extended. The doubling of mouth-and-teaching reinforces the Exodus background of God supplying words to those summoned before rulers. Recurrence strengthens the Mosaic echo.

echoes.text: Then answered they and said before the king, That Daniel, who is of the children of the captivity of Judah, doesn’t respect you, O king, nor the decree that you have signed, but makes his petition three times a day. Then the king, when he heard these words, was very displeased, and set his heart on Daniel to deliver him; and he labored until the going down of the sun to rescue him. Then these men assembled together to the king, and said to the king, Know, […]
echoes.note: Daniel is brought before the king and delivered up on account of his fidelity, a model of the faithful Jew arraigned before pagan authority who is nonetheless preserved. Jesus' 'bringing you before kings and governors for my name's sake' as occasion for testimony evokes the Danielic court-confessor tradition. Coherence with Daniel's witness motif.

echoes.text: He shall speak words against the Most High, and shall wear out the saints of the Most High; and he shall think to change the times and the law; and they shall be given into his hand until a time and times and half a time.
echoes.note: The little horn wears out the saints of the Most High, who are given into his hand for a time. Jesus' forecast of persecution, betrayal, and death of his followers fits the Danielic pattern of the saints handed over before final vindication. Recurrence within the apocalyptic source of the discourse.

echoes.text: Then she said, “Please let the king remember Yahweh your God, that the avenger of blood destroy not any more, lest they destroy my son.” He said, “As Yahweh lives, not one hair of your son shall fall to the earth.”
echoes.note: The wise woman of Tekoa secures David's oath that 'not one hair of your son shall fall to the ground,' the same idiom of total protection. The recurrence of the hair-of-the-head formula across Samuel reinforces its proverbial status behind Jesus' saying. Coherence with the OT preservation idiom.

echoes.text: Solomon said, “If he shows himself a worthy man, not a hair of him shall fall to the earth; but if wickedness be found in him, he shall die.”
echoes.note: Solomon declares that if Adonijah proves worthy, 'not one of his hairs shall fall to the earth.' A third occurrence of the hair-preservation formula, confirming it as a fixed Hebrew idiom Jesus deploys. Faint but corroborating recurrence.

echoes.text: Blessed is he who waits, and comes to the one thousand three hundred thirty-five days. But go you your way until the end; for you shall rest, and shall stand in your lot, at the end of the days.
echoes.note: Daniel is told, 'blessed is he who waits' and to stand in his lot at the end of days, framing endurance as the path to eschatological reward. Jesus' 'by your endurance you will win your lives' resonates with this Danielic call to persevere to the resurrection-end. Thematic coherence with apocalyptic endurance.
